front: Virtualization: where and when did the idea originate, and what problem did it solve?
back: It originated in the 1960s at IBM, when computing meant a few large mainframes shared by many users. It let multiple operating systems concurrently run on the same physical hardware, so diverse workloads did not all have to use one OS.

front: What is a virtual machine (VM), and what are its other names?
back: A VM is an operating system plus its applications and its virtual resources. Each OS deployed on the shared platform has the illusion it owns the underlying hardware. VMs are also called guests or domains.

text: The virtualization layer is also called a {{c1::virtual machine monitor}} or {{c2::hypervisor}}.
extra: It provides allocation and management of real hardware resources and isolation guarantees across VMs.

front: Defining virtualization: complete the definition. A virtual machine is an efficient, isolated ___ of a real machine.
back: An efficient, isolated duplicate of a real machine.

front: What are the three responsibilities of the VMM in the lecture's framing?
back:
• Fidelity: provide an environment essentially identical to the original machine (same CPU/device types; capacity may differ)
  • Performance: VM programs show at worst only minor speed decreases, as close to native as possible
  • Safety and isolation: the VMM is in complete control of resources, deciding who accesses what and when; it does not inspect every hardware access, but decides whether a VM gets direct hardware access, and a VM cannot change those policies to hurt co-located VMs

front: Defining virtualization: lecture names the VMM properties fidelity, performance, safety. What three formal properties does the Popek & Goldberg paper name instead?
back:
• Equivalence: any program runs with an effect identical to running on bare metal, except for timing and resource-availability differences
  • Efficiency: a statistically dominant subset of instructions executes directly on the real processor with no VMM intervention
  • Resource control: a program cannot access resources not allocated to it, and under certain circumstances the VMM can regain control of resources already allocated

front: Popek & Goldberg: which property formally excludes pure emulators and interpreters from being VMMs, and which distinguishes a VMM from an ordinary time-sharing OS?
back: The efficiency property excludes pure emulators and software interpreters. The equivalence property distinguishes a VMM from an ordinary time-sharing OS and from plain virtual memory.

front: Virtualization tech quiz: by Popek and Goldberg's classical definition, which of VirtualBox, the Java Virtual Machine, and Virtual GameBoy are virtualization technologies, and why?
back: Only VirtualBox: with system virtualization the hardware visible to the VM is identical, or at least very similar, to the physical platform. The JVM is a language runtime providing system services and portability, very different from the physical machine. Virtual GameBoy emulates a different hardware platform (the GameBoy).

front: Virtualization benefit: what is consolidation, and what does it improve?
back: Consolidation is running multiple VMs on a single physical platform. It means fewer machines, less space, fewer admins, and smaller electric bills for the same workload, decreasing cost and improving manageability.

front: Benefits of virtualization: list the benefits besides consolidation.
back:
• Migration: OS/apps decoupled from the physical system, so easy to migrate from one machine to another, or to copy and clone onto multiple machines
  • Availability and reliability: create more VMs when load increases (availability); migrate VMs off a node that is getting hot and likely to fail (reliability)
  • Containment of bugs and malicious code: confined to their isolated VMs without bringing down other VMs or the platform
  • OS research: quickly boot and test OSes without restarting hardware
  • Legacy OS support: run old OSes as one VM among many

front: Why did virtualization lapse after the mainframe era, and why did it return?
back: It lapsed because mainframes were not ubiquitous and commodity x86 hardware was cheap: easier to buy another machine than to make OSes coexist (not because virtualization was inefficient, or because everyone used Microsoft Windows). It returned when data centers grew huge, servers sat at 10 to 20 percent utilization, admin headcount and power/cooling bills rose, and companies spent about 70 percent of IT budget on operating expenses.

front: Benefits of virtualization: Rosenblum & Garfinkel sharpen the historical arc. What combination both killed VMMs in the 1980s and later caused the problems VMMs solve?
back: Cheap hardware plus capable multitasking operating systems. Cheap hardware proliferated underused machines; more capable OSes grew fragile and vulnerable, pushing admins back to one-application-per-machine and so back to hardware sprawl.

front: Benefits of virtualization: how does Rosenblum & Garfinkel reframe the VMM's role going forward?
back: A VMM is less a vehicle for multitasking and more a solution for security and reliability. They argue functions like migration and security are better implemented at the VMM layer than inside today's complex and ossified operating systems.

front: Benefits of virtualization: name benefits the Rosenblum & Garfinkel paper lists that the lecture does not.
back:
• General-purpose undo via checkpoint and rollback
  • VMM-level security: intrusion detection (Livewire), after-the-fact break-in analysis (ReVirt)
  • High-assurance isolation (NSA NetTop)
  • Trusted computing with remote attestation (Terra)
  • Distributing preconfigured software stacks as virtual appliances

front: Benefits of virtualization: per Rosenblum & Garfinkel, how were VMMs regarded by the late 1980s?
back: As little more than a historical curiosity.

text: Bare-metal virtualization is also called {{c1::hypervisor-based}} or {{c2::type 1}} virtualization, where the VMM manages all hardware resources and supports VM execution.

front: Bare-metal virtualization: what device problem does it create, and how is it solved?
back: The hypervisor must manage all devices, so manufacturers must write drivers for different hypervisors, not just different OSes. The fix is a special service VM running a standardized OS with full hardware access privileges that runs all the device drivers and controls device use, plus other configuration and management tasks that assist the hypervisor.

front: Xen terminology: what are the privileged domain, the guest domains, and where do the device drivers run?
back: The privileged domain is dom0; guest domains are domUs. Xen is the hypervisor, and all device drivers run in dom0.

front: Bare-metal (type 1) virtualization: which products use it?
back: Xen and VMware's ESX hypervisor.

front: Bare-metal virtualization: how does VMware handle device drivers and configuration?
back: VMware holds the largest share of server cores, so it can mandate that device manufacturers write drivers usable by the hypervisor; since it targets servers, there are relatively few devices. It exports a number of APIs, both to support a third-party developer community and to let users configure exactly the policies the hypervisor enforces. It used to have a Linux-based control core (like Xen's dom0), but now all configuration is done via remote APIs.

text: The hosted virtualization model is also called {{c1::type 2}}: a full host OS manages the hardware and integrates a VMM that provides VMs their virtual platform interface.
extra: The VMM also manages context switching and scheduling, invoking host device drivers and other host components as needed.

front: Hosted (type 2) virtualization: what is the main benefit of the model?
back: It leverages the services and mechanisms already developed for the host OS, so much less functionality needs to be built into the VMM module. You can run guest VMs through the VMM and native applications directly on the host.

front: Hosted virtualization example: what is KVM, and what two components provide guest-VM support?
back: KVM (kernel-based VM) is built into Linux; the Linux host manages hardware and runs regular Linux apps directly. Guest-VM support comes from the KVM (VMM) module plus the hardware emulator QEMU, used in virtualizer mode: it does not emulate foreign hardware; the guest sees the exact physical hardware resources, and QEMU intervenes only on critical operations (e.g. I/O, since the host Linux handles all device drivers) to pass control to the KVM module and the host OS.

front: Hosted model: what advantage does KVM get from being built into Linux?
back: It leverages all the advances contributed by the Linux open-source community, so it quickly adapts to new features and fixes.

front: KVM history: why was the KVM module originally developed, and how did it become mainstream?
back: It was originally developed so regular Linux applications could use the virtualization-related hardware appearing in commodity platforms. Once users realized it could also run guest OSes and regular VMs, it became, three months later, a virtualization solution in the mainstream Linux kernel.

front: Hosted virtualization: lecture's example is KVM. What is Rosenblum & Garfinkel's canonical hosted example, and what does the virtualization layer reuse?
back: The paper's canonical example is VMware Workstation (its Figure 2; the term hosted architecture comes from the paper's reference on Workstation's hosted VMM, Sugerman et al.). The layer reuses the host OS's device drivers: a guest disk read/write becomes a host-filesystem file read/write via a system call, and the guest display renders into a window on the host.

front: Rosenblum & Garfinkel: what three advantages and what two disadvantages does the hosted architecture have, and what did they drive VMware to do?
back: Advantages: installs like an ordinary application (not on bare hardware), inherits the host's rich driver support for diverse x86 devices, and reuses the host's scheduling and resource management. Disadvantages: high I/O overhead, since every I/O crosses into the host and its software layers, and no host-provided performance isolation. Together they are why ESX Server dropped the host OS and runs on bare hardware.

front: Bare metal or hosted quiz: classify KVM, Fusion, VirtualBox, VMware Player, VMware ESX, Citrix XenServer, and Microsoft Hyper-V.
back:
• Bare-metal (hypervisor-based): VMware ESX, Citrix XenServer, Microsoft Hyper-V
  • Hosted: KVM, Fusion, VirtualBox, VMware Player
Caveat: in KVM the host OS switches into a module that assumes a hypervisor-like role, so the rest of the OS plays a secondary, supporting role, like a privileged partition.

front: Hardware protection levels: what four requirements follow from the definition of a virtualization solution?
back:
• Present a virtual platform interface over CPU, memory, and devices to each guest VM
  • Isolate guest VMs from one another
  • Preserve the guest OS's protection from faulty/malicious apps in the same VM
  • Protect the VMM from the guest OSes

front: Hardware protection levels: why can the guest OS and the VMM not run at the same protection level?
back: So a single faulty guest cannot take down the hypervisor and the whole machine. Protecting the guest OS from its apps and protecting the VMM from the guest OS together require them to sit at different levels. (Cross-VM isolation can reuse existing OS mechanisms like preemption and the MMU.)

front: x86 rings: how many protection levels does x86 have, and what resides at ring 0 and ring 3 natively?
back: x86 has four protection levels called rings. Ring 0 has the highest privilege (all resources, all instructions); natively the OS lives there. Ring 3 has the least privilege; applications live there, and an unprivileged operation traps to ring 0.

front: Virtualization ring layout: where do the hypervisor, OS, and applications sit on older x86 (rings only)?
back: The hypervisor sits in ring 0, which pushes the OS to ring 1, and applications remain at ring 3.

front: x86 protection modes: what are the two modes on newer x86, and how are rings and the hypervisor arranged?
back: Root and non-root modes, each containing the four rings. Root mode permits everything, with the hypervisor in ring 0 of root mode. Guest VMs run in non-root mode: OS in ring 0, applications in ring 3.

text: When a guest OS attempts a privileged operation it causes a trap called a {{c1::VMExit}} that switches to root mode and passes control to the hypervisor; control returns to the VM via a {{c2::VMEntry}}, which switches out of root mode.

front: Processor virtualization: how are ordinary guest instructions handled, and why does this matter?
back: Guest instructions are executed directly by the hardware; the VMM does not interfere with every instruction. As long as the guest operates within its allocated resources, instructions run at hardware speeds, underlining the efficiency of virtualization.

front: What is the trap-and-emulate strategy?
back: When the guest issues a privileged instruction, the processor traps to the hypervisor. The hypervisor decides whether to allow it: if illegal, it may take punitive action (e.g. shut down the VM); if allowed, it emulates the instruction so the guest OS gets the expected hardware response. The intervention must be invisible to the guest OS.

front: Processor virtualization: Popek & Goldberg prove trap-and-emulate correct. What three parts make up the VMM in the paper's model?
back:
• Dispatcher: placed at the hardware trap entry point
  • Allocator: decides which resources a VM gets; invoked whenever a trapped instruction would change a VM's resources
  • Interpreter routines: one per privileged instruction, simulating the trapped instruction's effect

front: Popek & Goldberg: define privileged, sensitive (control vs behavior), and innocuous instructions.
back:
• Privileged: traps in user mode but not in supervisor mode
  • Control sensitive: changes available resources or changes processor mode without the memory-trap sequence
  • Behavior sensitive: its result depends on resource configuration, i.e. location in real memory (location sensitivity) or processor mode (mode sensitivity)
  • Innocuous: any instruction that is not sensitive

front: Popek & Goldberg Theorem 1: under what condition can a VMM be constructed for a third-generation machine, and why?
back: A VMM can be constructed if the set of sensitive instructions is a subset of the set of privileged instructions. That guarantees every instruction the VMM must mediate will trap. This is the formal statement the lecture compresses into "privileged instructions trap".

front: x86 virtualization before 2005: what was the ring strategy, and what was the core problem?
back: Only the four rings existed (no root/non-root). Strategy: hypervisor in ring 0, guest OS in ring 1. The problem: exactly 17 instructions were privileged (needed ring 0) but did not trap, so issuing them from another level failed silently instead of passing control to the hypervisor.

front: x86 past: give the concrete example of the silent-failure problem with the 17 instructions.
back: Enabling/disabling interrupts means flipping a bit in a privileged register via POPF/PUSHF. Issued outside ring 0 they failed silently: the hypervisor never saw the attempt (so could not emulate it), and the OS never saw the failure (so assumed success and continued).

front: x86 past: lecture says "privileged instructions that do not trap". How does Popek & Goldberg's vocabulary correct this, and where does the count 17 come from?
back: The precise statement is that the 17 are sensitive but not privileged: they read or change privileged state (sensitive) yet do not trap outside ring 0 (not privileged). A privileged instruction is by definition one that traps. They violate Theorem 1's subset condition. The count of 17 is not from the paper; it comes from Robin and Irvine's USENIX Security 2000 analysis of the roughly 250 Pentium instructions.

front: x86 past: what two concrete x86 examples does Rosenblum & Garfinkel give for the non-virtualizable-instruction problem?
back:
• POPF (pop flags): used to set/clear the interrupt-disable flag, but unprivileged it does not trap; it silently ignores the change to the interrupt flag, breaking direct execution of kernel code
  • Reading privileged state: a guest reads the code-segment register to see the current privilege level; the read does not trap, so the VMM cannot patch it and the guest sees the wrong (physical) privilege level, not its virtual one

front: x86 past quiz: with POPF/PUSHF failing silently outside ring 0, could the guest request interrupts enabled, request them disabled, or read the interrupt-enabled bit? What can happen next?
back: None of them succeeds (quiz answer: all of the above can occur): each needs the privileged flags register. The guest assumes the request completed and may misinterpret other stack data as the register's value. It may then run code that, if interrupted, leaves it in a corrupt or deadlocked state, so trap-and-emulate is not applicable to pre-2005 x86.

front: What is binary translation, and what goal does it pursue?
back: Binary translation rewrites the VM binary so it never issues the 17 bad instructions, intercepting and translating instruction sequences at the virtualization layer. Its goal is to run unmodified guest operating systems; when the guest is unmodified this is called full virtualization.

front: Binary translation: describe the runtime process on a code block.
back: At runtime (dynamically, because the execution sequence is input dependent, so it cannot be done efficiently statically up front), code blocks about to execute, typically a basic block such as a loop or a function, are captured and inspected for the 17 bad instructions. If none are present, the block is marked safe and runs at hardware speed. If a bad instruction is found, it is translated into an alternate instruction sequence that emulates the desired behavior.

front: Binary translation: what overheads does it add, and how are they reduced? Who pioneered it?
back: It adds translation overhead, reduced by caching translated code fragments and only analyzing kernel code executed in the guest. It was taken by VMware and pioneered by the Stanford group led by Mendel Rosenblum, a VMware co-founder and co-author of the Rosenblum and Garfinkel paper. He was later named an ACM Fellow for reinventing virtualization, was VMware's chief scientist for about ten years, and is now back full time at Stanford.

front: Binary translation: what extra detail does Rosenblum & Garfinkel give about VMware's implementation and the trace cache?
back: Only privileged (kernel) code runs under the translator; each block is translated into a similar block with problematic instructions replaced, and the result is cached in a trace cache so a block is translated only on first execution. Output looks much like paravirtualization (normal instructions unchanged, POPF and code-segment reads replaced), but changes apply at first execution rather than to the OS source.

front: Binary translation: why does Rosenblum & Garfinkel call it a performance optimization, not just a correctness fix?
back: It can remove frequently-trapping privileged instructions, cutting trap overhead that is especially high on the deep pipelines of modern x86 CPUs. VMware's translation is also simpler than cross-ISA translators because source and target instruction sets are nearly identical. Once the trace cache is warm, performance is nearly indistinguishable from direct execution.

front: What is paravirtualization, and what is a hypercall?
back: Paravirtualization gives up unmodified guests for performance: the guest OS is modified so it knows it runs on a hypervisor, not native hardware. A hypercall is an explicit call to the hypervisor requesting a hardware manipulation, similar to a system call: the guest packages its context and state, specifies the desired hypercall, and issues it; the hypercall traps to the hypervisor, which performs the operation with the supplied data and passes control (and any data) back to the guest.

front: Paravirtualization: lecture's example is Xen. What is Rosenblum & Garfinkel's canonical example, and how is paravirtualization framed generally?
back: The paper's canonical example is Disco, a VMM for the non-virtualizable MIPS architecture (Xen is not discussed). Disco replaced the MIPS equivalents of POPF and the code-segment read with accesses to a special memory location, removing traps and improving performance. Generally, the VMM builder replaces the non-virtualizable parts of the instruction set with easily virtualized equivalents, so apps run unmodified but the OS must be ported.

front: Paravirtualization: what is its main drawback per Rosenblum & Garfinkel, and what does that imply about who used it?
back: The main drawback is incompatibility: a ported OS, vendor cooperation, no legacy operating systems, and no easy migration of existing machines. In spite of that drawback, academic projects favored paravirtualization, because building a VMM with both full compatibility and high performance is a significant engineering challenge; VMware, aiming at fast, compatible x86 virtualization, built binary translation instead.

front: x86 virtualization problem: how does paravirtualization deal with the 17 privileged instructions that fail silently instead of trapping?
back: It is the second way to deal with them (after binary translation). Rather than rewriting the guest binary at runtime, the guest OS is modified so it does not issue the problematic instructions (e.g. POPF from ring 1) and instead makes explicit hypercalls to the hypervisor to request the hardware manipulation. Originally adopted and popularized by Xen.

front: Xen history: where did Xen start, and what happened to it commercially?
back: It started as an open source research project at the University of Cambridge (UK), was commercialized as XenSource, now owned by Citrix. The open source Xen project remains active, and the open source and Citrix versions have diverged over time.

front: BT and PV quiz: which traps to the hypervisor in both binary-translated and paravirtualized VMs: access to a swapped-out page, or an update to a page table entry?
back: Access to a swapped-out page: the page is not present, so the hardware MMU faults and passes control to the hypervisor regardless of the approach. A page table entry update does not always trap; it depends on whether the guest OS has write permission to the page tables it uses.

front: Memory virtualization (full): what must the guest OS continue to observe, and what three address types are distinguished?
back: The guest OS must observe a contiguous, linear address space starting at zero, as if it owned physical memory. Three address types: virtual addresses (used by guest applications), physical addresses (used by the guest kernel), and machine addresses (the real physical platform addresses).

front: Memory virtualization (full): what two mappings/page tables exist, and why is the naive two-level translation too expensive?
back: The guest OS maps virtual to physical addresses (the physical it thinks it owns); the hypervisor maps physical to machine addresses (contiguous physical can map to discontiguous machine). So there are two page tables. The first translation exists solely in software; only the second can leverage the MMU and TLB, so doing both on every memory reference adds too much overhead.

front: Memory virtualization (full): what is a shadow page table and how is consistency maintained?
back: The hypervisor keeps a shadow page table that maps virtual directly to machine addresses, skipping physical. The hardware MMU uses the shadow table, so the guest runs natively, completely transparently to the guest OS. To stay consistent it must invalidate the shadow table on context switch and write-protect the guest page table, so that when the guest adds a mapping it traps into the hypervisor, which then updates the shadow table.

front: Shadow page tables: Rosenblum & Garfinkel adds two capabilities the lecture omits. What is the first, about memory overcommit and ballooning?
back: Because the VMM controls the shadow page table it can page a VM out to disk and overcommit machine memory (total VM memory exceeds physical). The VMM lacks the guest's knowledge of good eviction candidates, so ESX Server uses a balloon process (today usually called a balloon driver) in the guest: to reclaim memory the VMM inflates the balloon and the guest, using its own page-replacement knowledge, picks pages to surrender.

front: Shadow page tables: what is the second capability Rosenblum & Garfinkel describes, content-based page sharing?
back: Running many similar VMs wastes memory on identical pages. ESX Server uses content-based page sharing: the VMM detects identical physical pages, points the shadow page tables at a single copy, and copies on write if contents later diverge (e.g. 30 Windows VMs needing only one in-memory kernel copy). The paper flags hardware-managed shadow page tables as a promising future direction.

front: Memory virtualization (paravirtualization): how does it simplify the page-table setup, and what protects the table?
back: The guest OS need not use contiguous physical memory starting at 0; it can explicitly register its page tables with the hypervisor, so there is no need for two page tables. The guest still lacks write permission to this table (now used directly by hardware), preventing it from corrupting another guest.

front: Memory virtualization (paravirtualization): how is page-table-update trap cost reduced?
back: Every page-table write still traps to the hypervisor, but because the guest is paravirtualized it can be modified to batch page table updates into a single hypercall, amortizing the VM-exit cost across many updates. Other optimizations are possible, e.g. memory management made friendlier to virtualized execution or more cooperative with other VMs. Newer hardware has further reduced these overheads.

front: Device virtualization: why are devices harder to virtualize than CPU and memory?
back: CPU/memory virtualization benefits from strong standardization at the ISA level (e.g. x86), so lower-level hardware differences do not matter. Devices have far greater diversity and a lack of standardization in device interfaces and their semantics.

front: How many models exist to virtualize devices, and what are they?
back: Three models: the passthrough model, the hypervisor-direct model, and the split device driver model. They were developed before virtualization-friendly CPU and chipset extensions, which later made some aspects of device virtualization much simpler.

front: Device virtualization: how does Rosenblum & Garfinkel frame the history, and what did x86 lose from mainframes?
back: Thirty years ago IBM mainframes used a channel-based I/O architecture, where a separate channel processor let the VMM export device access directly to the VM with very low overhead. x86 lost this: its huge, diverse device collection makes a VMM I/O layer a large effort, and some devices (graphics, high-speed network) have severe performance requirements.

front: Device virtualization: what three I/O approaches do Rosenblum & Garfinkel describe, and how far do they line up with the note's three device models?
back:
• Hosted architecture: routes I/O through the host OS drivers (highest overhead, VMware Workstation); matches none of the three models
  • ESX Server: traditional VMM borrowing Linux drivers directly (lower overhead); the hypervisor-direct model, feasible because relatively few server I/O devices are certified for major x86 server machines
  • Optimized paravirtualized virtual devices: match no real device and need a special guest driver; the split-device-driver idea
So they only partly line up: the last two do, the hosted approach does not.

front: Device virtualization: what future I/O support does Rosenblum & Garfinkel predict, and which device model does it make safe?
back: Channel-like devices (USB, SCSI) and hardware support (DMA address remapping, interrupt routing to the right VM) that let device drivers in the VM talk to the device directly with no trap into the VMM: the passthrough model made safe.

front: Passthrough (VMM-bypass) device model: how does it work and what is its performance benefit?
back: The VMM-level driver only configures access permissions (e.g. maps a device's memory registers to a guest). The guest then gets exclusive, direct access to the device without interacting with the VMM, so it is also called the VMM-bypass model. Benefit: the hypervisor is completely out of the way on device accesses; the guest's own driver operates and controls the device directly.

front: Passthrough device model: what are its two main drawbacks?
back:
• Hard to share: exclusive access means the hypervisor must continually reassign device ownership and access cannot be concurrent across VMs, often unfeasible
  • Breaks decoupling / migration: the device is bound to the VM and must be the exact same type on the physical platform; device-specific resident state must be copied/configured to the destination, reintroducing migration complexity

front: Hypervisor-direct device model: how does it process a guest device request?
back: The hypervisor intercepts every device access, translates it to a generic representation of an I/O operation for that device family (network, disk), traverses the hypervisor-resident I/O stack, and at the bottom invokes the real device driver. The requested and physical device no longer need to match.

front: Hypervisor-direct device model: what are its benefits and downsides?
back: Benefits: the VM stays decoupled from the platform (easy migration) and device sharing works since the hypervisor manages access. Downsides: the emulation step adds latency, and the hypervisor must support all drivers, exposing it to the complexity of various device drivers.

front: Hypervisor-direct device model: which hypervisor originally adopted it, and why was that reasonable?
back: VMware ESX. Because of VMware's market share, vendors provide drivers for its hypervisor, so requiring the hypervisor to support all drivers was reasonable for VMware, and the model has been sustained because of that.

front: Split device driver model: what are the front-end and back-end drivers, where do they live, and which must be modified?
back: The front-end driver lives in the guest VM; the back-end driver (the real physical-device driver) lives in the service VM (or the host in type 2). The back-end need not be modified, but the front-end must be modified to wrap guest device operations in special messages passed directly to the back-end in the service VM.

front: Split device driver model: why is it limited to paravirtualized guests, and what are its benefits?
back: Because the front-end driver must be modified, it can only be used in paravirtualized guests; guest applications need no change, since the front-end looks like a wrapper for the device API. Benefits: it eliminates device emulation overhead (the virtualization layer need not reverse engineer what the guest OS wants; the front-end tells it explicitly), and the centralized back-end allows better management of shared devices (e.g. finer-grained fairness and priority policies).

front: Hardware virtualization: what were the two x86 virtualization-friendly architectures introduced circa 2005?
back: The AMD Pacifica architecture and the Intel Vanderpool Technology architecture, both circa 2005.

front: Hardware virtualization: what did Rosenblum & Garfinkel (2005) predict about Vanderpool/Pacifica, and what did they forecast for paravirtualization?
back: They noted both had announced hardware support that, rather than making existing modes virtualizable, adds a new execution mode letting a VMM safely use direct execution, reducing both the number of traps and the cost of each. They forecast direct-execution-only VMMs become possible on x86 (at least for guests that do not themselves use the new modes), that support as good as IBM's mainframe support would cut overhead further and simplify implementation, and that a fully compatible VM abstraction's value would outweigh any performance benefit from breaking compatibility (i.e. from paravirtualization).

front: Hardware virtualization: closing the 17-instruction holes is Popek & Goldberg's Theorem 1 in action. Explain.
back: Forcing the 17 sensitive-but-unprivileged instructions to trap moves them into the privileged set, so the set of sensitive instructions becomes a subset of the privileged instructions. Theorem 1's condition is satisfied, so the trap-and-emulate VMM the paper proves constructible can again be built, now directly in hardware rather than worked around by binary translation.

front: Hardware virtualization: what per-vCPU control structure did hardware add, and what are its Intel and AMD names?
back: A per-vCPU control structure holding virtual-processor state: the VM control structure (VMCS) on Intel and the VM control block (VMCB) on AMD. The hardware can walk this structure and specify whether a given system call should trap, so that operation need not trap into root mode and can instead be handled by the guest OS (the privileged layer in non-root mode).

front: Hardware virtualization: what did tagging memory structures with VM identifiers enable, and what are world switches?
back: It led to extended page tables and tagged TLBs carrying VM identifiers. This makes world switches (context switches between VMs) more efficient: the previous VM's TLB entries no longer have to be flushed, because the MMU matches both the virtual address and the VM identifier against each entry and uses it only if both match.

front: Hardware virtualization: what I/O virtualization extensions were added to the processor and chipset?
back:
• Multiqueue devices: one device with multiple logical interfaces usable by multiple VMs
  • Better interrupt routing: so the core running the VM is the core that gets interrupted

front: Hardware virtualization: besides making the 17 instructions trap and adding the per-vCPU control structure, what other processor-level changes were made?
back:
• A new protection mode: root and non-root (a.k.a. host and guest)
  • Features for better security (protecting VMs from one another and from the hypervisor) and better management support
  • New x86 instructions to implement the new features, e.g. one to switch into the new protection mode, and others to manipulate state in the per-VM control structure

front: Hardware virtualization quiz: with hardware support, guests run unmodified and can access the devices. Is the split device driver model still relevant?
back: Yes. All device requests are consolidated in the service VM, which can make better decisions and enforce stronger policies about how the device is shared, without relying on the physical device to support the desired sharing behavior.

front: x86 VT revolution: what are Intel's three dimensions of virtualization support and their brand names?
back:
• CPU: fix non-virtualizable instructions, add extended page tables; branded VT-x (later VT-x2, VT-x3)
  • Chipset: I/O virtualization, I/O routing, direct device access (e.g. SR-IOV at platform level); branded VT-d
  • Devices: DMA remapping (DMA into the correct VM's memory), multiple logical interfaces/queues per VM; branded IOV and VMDq
